text: This interview was held telephonically with Mr. Bruce D'Armond on Sunday, February 15, 1998, at 5 o'clock p.m., Mountain Daylight Time.
Interviewer is W.A. Connors, a private researcher specializing in the history of Project Sign.

Albert B. DeArmond was a member of the Project Signed team, which was located at Air Materiel
Command's Intelligence Division, Wright-Patterson Air Force Base in Dayton, Ohio, from late
1947 until mid-1949.
He was co-author with Mr. Lawrence Trutner of the team's technical report entitled, Unidentified
Aerial Objects, Project Signed.
Hi Bruce, thank you very much for taking time to reflect on your father's life.
Could you tell me a little about yourself?
My name is Albert Bruce DeArmond.
I was born November 28, 1949, Cook County Hospital in Chicago, Illinois.
I was premature and stayed in the hospital for two weeks.
Then I was adopted by Albert Bonnell DeArmond and Christine Bruce DeArmond, who lived in Dayton, Ohio.
They took me there.
and to my recollection I stayed there until 1952.
I could be off a little bit.
Then we moved to Alcahon, California.
We stayed there until I was in first grade.
I think that was 1956 or 57.
We moved to Santa Barbara, California
and I stayed there until about 1970
1970, and I moved to Northern California.
What do you do for a living now, Bruce?
Right now I'm a drug and alcohol counselor at Bridge Counseling in Las Vegas, Nevada.
Oh, that sounds like a very interesting job.
It's pretty rewarding.
I'm sure it is.
Could you give me some insight into your father, who he was, any recollections about him,
what did he look like, that kind of thing?

Well, my father was about 6'2". He weighed probably 240. Big, tall guy, real happy. He was bald just like I'll be in a few years. He was extremely intelligent and a lot of the times I felt like he had to talk down to me.
He was a good guy, but he wasn't real touchy-feely.
I think he was more intellectual than he was emotional.
He always was real guarded with his emotions.
But he treated me very well, stood by me through lots of problems.
I was a drug addict for years and he always hung right in there with me and tried his
best to get me out of trouble.
Could you tell me where he was born? Was he an American citizen or was he naturalized?
He was naturalized. He was born in Nova Scotia and I don't really know what city or what town or what farm he was born on.
His father's name was George DeArmond and his mother's name, I'm sorry, I don't remember it. I would have to look it up.
they moved to Canton, Massachusetts, where his father was a maintenance engineer or some kind of engineer for a factory, I believe.
It's real sketchy.
And he grew up there.
I believe he was, and I'm guessing at this, in junior high or maybe high school.
graduated from Canton High School in 1926.
Did he attend college?
He attended MIT and graduated with a Bachelor of Science in Aeronautical Engineering in June of 1930.
Oh, cool.
What did he like to do when he wasn't working?
Well, he liked to fly, actually, and he has a commercial pilot's license,
but I'm not sure what ever developed on that.
Possibly my mother didn't like him flying. I'm not sure.
I found a little card that said he had a commercial pilot's license today.
Did you ever fly with him?
I think I did, but I was very, very young,
and there may have been some sort of incident that I don't know about that stopped him from flying.
Maybe it was your mom.
Yeah.
What did he like to do besides flying?
Well, he really liked working in the yard. When we lived in El Cajon, he put in a swimming
pool and he pretty much did the whole thing. When we lived in Santa Barbara, he was always,
every weekend he was out there working in the yard and planting trees and doing all
kinds of stuff. He liked going to the beach. He liked to swim in the ocean.
Oh, so he was an avid swimmer.
Yes. He always took us on pretty nice vacations.
I mean, we went to Mexico and Hawaii and all over the western United States to almost all the national parks.
He was pretty active outdoors.
However, he was pretty 9 to 5 Monday through Friday.
And that would go on for months and then we'd have a two-week vacation in the middle of summer.
Your father, from what I understand, you know, there was a question I wanted to ask.
Okay.
What color were his eyes?
His eyes were blue.
His hair was red.
Red?
When he was younger, and I believe he had the nickname Red.
I was adopted when he was 40 years old.
He was bald and had gray hair at that point.
So I just know that he had red hair because I had heard stories,
and I think he told me that his name was Red.
Did he ever mention a person's name by the name of Red Honaker?
Not to my knowledge.
Not to your knowledge.
Your father was in the Army Air Forces during World War II, from what I understand.
Could you tell me what his rank was?
He was in the Army Air Corps, and he would always tell me it was called the Army Air Corps back then.
And he went in as an officer, I believe, in World War II.
According to documentation I found recently, he was a captain, I believe, at the end of the war,
and then he was promoted to a lieutenant colonel, and his final rank was full colonel.

My father never talked to me about it.
My mother did after he passed away.

I was really young, and I pretty much walked in my sleep for years.
I've since stopped.
But apparently I got up and took a header down the stairs.
Oh, wow.
I used to walk in my sleep, and one time my father told me that I ended up headfirst in a wastebasket.
All they could do was hear me, but they could never find me for about an hour.
So I guess maybe we both walked that same path in the middle of the night on many occasions.

He never brought it up.

Probably 15 years older than me or somewhere in there.

I said, look, you're a scientist, you're an intellectual man.
Tell me about Flying Saucers and tell me about this Blue Book project.

and I'll gladly tell you the whole story, which I replied, I won't even be around in 2025, so tell me now.
and he just kept saying it'll be declassified in the year 2025.

Absolutely.

Absolutely, close-lipped on what he did because he had top security clearance
and he was really ethical.
I mean, he wouldn't cross that line.
And to tell you the truth, I never saw my father drunk.
wine occasionally at Thanksgiving and Christmas. He just was pretty close to the chest about

Presbyterian.
He was a Presbyterian.

He had high morals.

After he left Wright-Patterson, did he go anywhere else?
He went back to Ryan Aeronautical in San Diego, California,
and he stayed with them until I believe it was either 1956 or 1957.
And then we moved to Santa Barbara where he got a job at Tempo Technical Military Planning Operation.
It's a division of General Electric.
And from what I know of that time, he worked on stress analysis and guidance for the Polaris missile.
He did a lot of work with the Apollo capsule.
I assume he did some work with Mercury and Gemini, but I don't remember him ever saying that.
And he worked there until 1971 or 2.
industry. He didn't technically get laid off, but he sort of worked for Tempo and he also

take me.

I was in school, he said.
Oh, you were in school.

Could you tell me a little bit about how your father died, or when he retired and how he
died?
He retired, I believe, in 1971. It may have been 1972. He moved from Santa Barbara to
California. I lived a few miles up the hill from Sonora in a place called Cedar Ridge.
He moved there because my sister lived in Oakdale, which was about 35 miles from there.
and my adoptive parents, I call them my mother and father because they were,
they moved there and they bought a house.
I didn't notice a lot of shift in his awareness and what was going on,
but towards the end of the 70s, we thought that senility was setting in,
because he would forget stuff, and it was pretty gradual.
And by 1980, when he died, he was diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease,
so he may have been diagnosed, in fact, in the late 70s with it.
But he was pretty scattered at the end.
He would put the wrong shoe on the wrong foot and he would wander off and just start walking.
It was pretty frightening for my mother and pretty frightening for me, too.
I didn't have a lot of contact.
Even though I lived close by, I was pretty wild.
I would see him maybe once every month or so.
and I was going to school in Merced, so I was driving 90 miles one way to school all the time,
and I would just stop by occasionally.
I did notice that his awareness level and his cognitive ability had diminished rapidly,
and I have to admit I was pretty scared of the whole thing, and I limited my contact,
which is regrettable.
